overview: This file concerns American official monitoring of Japan’s English-language press and its treatment of the United States in 1940–1941. Its principal item is Ambassador Joseph C. Grew’s August 1940 despatch transmitting three Japan Times cartoons about President Franklin D. Roosevelt and American policy; it also contains an April 1940 State Department memorandum on the financing, staffing, ownership, and political orientation of the Japan Times and Japan Advertiser. Later-filed material includes cross-reference sheets and a November 1941 telegram reproducing the American Embassy’s published denial that the United States had demanded Chinese naval bases and economic concessions. Collectively, the documents illuminate press propaganda, foreign influence over newspapers, worsening U.S.–Japanese relations, and the Embassy’s efforts to answer hostile or misleading publicity.

people.name: Joseph C. Grew
people.role: U.S. Ambassador to Japan; sender of the despatch and telegram

people.name: Toshi Go
people.role: Managing Director and Editor of the Japan Times from January 10, 1940

subfiles.title: Grew despatch transmitting three Japan Times cartoons
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits and assesses three Japan Times cartoons concerning the United States and President Roosevelt.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards cartoons published on July 26, July 30, and August 2, 1940. He regards the first, concerning Roosevelt’s warning, as relatively unobjectionable, but calls the second unpleasant for portraying Roosevelt as allowing gasoline to Russia while denying it to Japan. He likewise objects to the third cartoon’s implication that the President was excessively talkative, noting Japanese sensitivity to derogatory treatment of a chief of state.

subfiles.title: “Uncle Sam’s Shadow” cartoon
subfiles.about: A Japan Times cartoon presents the United States as being awakened by Roosevelt’s warning.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure is a copy of a Japan Times cartoon captioned “Uncle Sam’s Shadow,” with text referring to “Roosevelt’s Warning.” Grew’s covering despatch interprets it as showing the United States awakening in response to the President’s warning and considers it not especially objectionable.

subfiles.title: Cartoon portraying Roosevelt as a gasoline pump
subfiles.about: A Japan Times cartoon caricatures Roosevelt as dispensing gasoline to Russia while withholding it from Japan.
subfiles.summary: The surviving enclosure page identifies the item as a Japan Times cartoon of July 30, 1940, although its pictorial content is not captured in the OCR. Grew describes it as showing the President’s head on a gasoline pump and insinuating that he craftily permitted Russia, but not Japan, to obtain gasoline. He characterizes the cartoon as distinctly unpleasant.

subfiles.title: “Coast Defenses” cartoon
subfiles.from: The Japan Times, reproducing material attributed to the New York Herald Tribune
subfiles.about: The cartoon and accompanying note criticize Roosevelt’s alleged talkativeness and identify the New Deal as an opposition target.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure reproduces a cartoon titled “Coast Defenses,” attributed to the New York Herald Tribune and published in the Japan Times. An accompanying note calls the Herald-Tribune anti-administration and says opposition critics were emphasizing Roosevelt’s alleged talkativeness, with the New Deal as their main target. Grew considered the implication of presidential garrulity unpleasant.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on alleged American demands in China
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew (sender of referenced telegram)
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a telegram quoting the Embassy’s denial of rumors that the United States demanded four Chinese naval bases and economic concessions in return for aid.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference records the subject as an alleged American demand to maintain and use four naval bases in China in exchange for Lend-Lease assistance. It directs researchers to Grew’s telegram no. 1748 of November 5, 1941, filed under 893.24/1193, which quotes an Embassy letter published in the Japan Times and Advertiser.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram reproducing Embassy denial of demands on China
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits the text of an Embassy letter denying press allegations that the United States sought Chinese naval bases and economic domination.
subfiles.summary: The telegram reproduces a letter published in the Japan Times and Advertiser in response to an October 31 editorial. The editorial had alleged that Washington demanded exclusive postwar use of four unnamed naval bases and economic measures that would give the United States virtual control over China. The Embassy declares both charges wholly imaginary and asks the editor to bring its denial to readers’ attention; the message was sent to the Department through Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on hostile Japanese press tone
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew (sender of referenced telegram)
subfiles.about: The sheet refers researchers to Grew’s report of informal comments to the Japanese foreign minister about aggressive press treatment of the United States.
subfiles.summary: This sheet cross-references telegram no. 1765 of November 7, 1941, filed under 711.94/2422. Its subject is the prevalent and increasingly aggressive tone of the Japanese press toward the United States and Grew’s authorized informal remarks about it during a meeting with the foreign minister. The referenced telegram itself is not included here.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the English-language press in Tokyo
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State (drafting notation: Coville)
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes intelligence about the editorial direction, financing, staffing, and prospective ownership of Tokyo’s English-language newspapers.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reports that under managing director and editor Toshi Go, the Japan Times was trying to present Japanese policy in ways appealing to American opinion and was recruiting American journalists at increased salaries. An informant claimed that the Japanese Foreign Office subsidized the paper by at least 7,000 yen monthly. Information attributed to the Fleishers also described Asahi interest in buying the Japan Advertiser, a German offer of $500,000 payable in New York, and a British Embassy proposal to purchase a 49 percent interest.

interest: The file is especially useful because it joins the visible products of press politics—the cartoons and published Embassy letter—to confidential assessments of newspaper funding, staffing, and possible acquisition. Grew’s comments also expose a diplomatic double standard he found striking: Japanese newspapers could caricature Roosevelt even though Japanese official culture was acutely sensitive to criticism of its own chief of state. The 1941 additions document the rapid shift from media monitoring to direct rebuttal of inflammatory claims immediately before the Pacific War, while the cross-reference sheets preserve links between press-related material scattered across different decimal-file subjects.
